{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/System/Type classes and instance resolution|Lean theorem prover/System/Lake and Lean projects}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A proof assistant without a library can prove only what someone has first defined from nothing.
This page describes what Lean users build on: the libraries that come with Lean, and Mathlib, the
community's library of mathematics. It says what Mathlib is, how it grows, how changes to it are
reviewed, how it is organised, and how a project obtains it.

== What comes with Lean ==

Lean arrives with a core library: natural numbers, integers, lists, arrays, strings, and the
logic and tactics used throughout this edition. It also ships a library named <code>Std</code>,
with data structures for programs, such as the lookup table <code>Std.HashMap</code>:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
import Std.Data.HashMap

#eval ((∅ : Std.HashMap String Nat).insert "one" 1).get? "one"
#eval [3, 1, 2].reverse
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints <code>some 1</code> and <code>[2, 1, 3]</code>. A further community library,
Batteries, describes itself as the "batteries included" extended library for Lean 4, with data
structures and tactics for both programming and mathematics.<ref name="batteries">''Batteries'' (README). [https://github.com/leanprover-community/batteries github.com/leanprover-community/batteries], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>

What core Lean does not have is most of mathematics. It does not even have the real numbers:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check Real
</pre>

Lean answers: Unknown identifier `Real`. The real numbers, and almost everything built on them,
come from Mathlib.

== Mathlib ==

'''Mathlib''' is a single, unified library of mathematics formalised in Lean, built by a community
rather than by one research group. A paper of 2020 describing it, written by "the mathlib Community", stressed
its focus on classical mathematics, its large hierarchy of mathematical structures, and its
distributed organisation.<ref name="cpp2020">The mathlib Community, "The Lean mathematical library", in ''Proceedings of the 9th ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Certified Programs and Proofs (CPP 2020)'', ACM, 2020, pp. 367–381. [https://doi.org/10.1145/3372885.3373824 doi:10.1145/3372885.3373824]; also arXiv:1910.09336.</ref>
It was begun in 2017.<ref name="growing">Anne Baanen, Matthew R. Ballard, Johan Commelin, Bryan Gin-ge Chen, Michael Rothgang and Damiano Testa, "Growing Mathlib: maintenance of a large scale mathematical library", arXiv:2508.21593, version 2, 7 October 2025; to appear at the Conference on Intelligent Computer Mathematics (CICM) 2025. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21593 arxiv.org/abs/2508.21593]</ref>
It was first written for Lean 3 and later translated to Lean 4 (see
[[Lean theorem prover/History/Mathlib and its community|Mathlib and its community]]).

Its size has been reported at several dates, each counted in its own way:

* in the 2020 paper (figures of 2019): 140,000 lines of code, not counting blank lines and comments, from 73 contributors, with 11 maintainers;<ref name="cpp2020" />
* in a paper of 2025 on Mathlib's maintenance: 1.9 million lines of code, with about 30 maintainers;<ref name="growing" />
* on the community's statistics page, consulted on 14 October 2026: 137,993 definitions, 290,354 theorems and 772 contributors.<ref name="stats">Lean community, "Mathlib statistics". [https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib_stats.html leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib_stats.html], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>

The 2020 paper gives a reason, drawn from mathematics itself, for one library rather than
many: its topics are intertwined, and rather than each building a separate project on a small common core,
the mathematicians involved joined their work to each other's and to Mathlib.<ref name="cpp2020" />

== How changes are reviewed ==

Anyone may propose a change to Mathlib, and everyone is allowed, and encouraged, to review the
changes others propose. A reviewer who is satisfied passes the change to the maintainers, who have
the final say; in the year before the 2025 paper on Mathlib's maintenance, about one change in three that was
accepted had first been approved by a reviewer in this way. Automatic checks called linters point
out common mistakes before a person looks.<ref name="growing" /> The 2020 paper describes the
same open arrangement: design is discussed in public, with little central control over what the
library contains.<ref name="cpp2020" />

Review is what makes a shared library trustworthy in the sense that matters for
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Stating the right thing|stating the right thing]]: a definition that
many people have read and used is more likely to mean what it says than one written for a single
proof.

== Organised by structures ==

Much of mathematics is organised by structures: a group, a ring, a field, an ordered field, a
topological space. A theorem proved for every group holds for each particular group. Mathlib
expresses each structure as a '''type class''': a description of what a type must provide, which
Lean finds automatically for a particular type when a theorem needs it.<ref name="cpp2020" /> A
small version, in core Lean:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
class Semigroup' (α : Type) extends Mul α where
  mul_assoc : ∀ a b c : α, a * b * c = a * (b * c)

theorem regroup {α : Type} [Semigroup' α] (a b c d : α) :
    a * b * c * d = a * (b * (c * d)) := by
  rw [Semigroup'.mul_assoc, Semigroup'.mul_assoc]

instance : Semigroup' Nat where
  mul_assoc := Nat.mul_assoc

instance : Semigroup' Int where
  mul_assoc := Int.mul_assoc

example (a b c d : Nat) : a * b * c * d = a * (b * (c * d)) := regroup a b c d
example (a b c d : Int) : a * b * c * d = a * (b * (c * d)) := regroup a b c d
</pre>

The class says what a semigroup is: a multiplication in which brackets can be moved. The theorem
<code>regroup</code> is proved once, for every semigroup. The two instances declare that natural
numbers and integers are semigroups, and the last two lines use the one theorem for both; Lean
finds the right instance itself. Lean accepts all of it.

Mathlib's version of this is large. Its class for fields, for instance, has 19 fields that carry
data, and keeping the automatic search for instances fast is a continuing part of the work of
maintaining it.<ref name="growing" />

== Getting a library ==

A Lean project obtains its libraries through '''Lake''', the tool that comes with Lean for
compiling Lean code and fetching what it depends on. A project names its dependencies; Lake records
the exact version of each in a file, <code>lake-manifest.json</code>, which Lean's reference says
should be kept with the project's own code; and before compiling, Lake brings each dependency to
the recorded version. The command <code>lake update</code> looks for newer versions, fetches them
and updates that record.<ref name="lake">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, section "Lake". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Lake/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Lake], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>

Rather than compile all of Mathlib from its source, a project can download Mathlib's compiled
files with a command the community provides, <code>lake exe cache get</code>. The community's
instructions also advise giving a project the same version of Lean as Mathlib uses.<ref name="install">Lean community, "Lean projects" (installation instructions). [https://leanprover-community.github.io/install/project.html leanprover-community.github.io/install/project.html], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>
Together with the version file described on
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Checking a proof again later|checking a proof again later]],
this fixes the version of everything a proof depends on.

Whether the project this wiki records will adopt Mathlib or stay with core Lean is one of its open
questions (see [[Principia Machina/Lean transition|the move to Lean]]).
